items.context: Joya de Cerén is a pre-Columbian farming village in the department of La Libertad, El Salvador. Around the year 600, the eruption of the nearby Loma Caldera volcano buried the village under several meters of volcanic ash. Because the inhabitants fled quickly, the site preserved houses, kitchens, storehouses and even cultivated fields of maize and manioc. The site was discovered in 1976, when a bulldozer uncovered the remains of a building during construction work. Systematic excavations began in 1978 under the direction of the archaeologist Payson Sheets. In 1993, Joya de Cerén was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List. It is often called the "Pompeii of the Americas" because it shows the daily life of ordinary farmers rather than the palaces of rulers.
items.question: Which volcano buried Joya de Cerén?

items.context: The Santa Ana Volcano, also known by its indigenous name Ilamatepec, is the highest volcano in El Salvador, with a summit elevation of about 2,381 meters. It is a stratovolcano located in the department of Santa Ana, west of the capital. Its summit contains a series of nested craters, and the innermost one holds a small acidic lake whose color changes from green to yellow. The most recent eruption took place on 1 October 2005; it threw rocks and ash over nearby coffee plantations and forced thousands of residents to evacuate. The volcano is part of the Los Volcanes National Park, together with the Izalco and Cerro Verde volcanoes. Hikers usually reach the crater in about two hours from the park entrance.
items.question: What is the indigenous name of the Santa Ana Volcano?

items.context: HTTP status codes tell a client how a server handled its request. Codes in the 2xx range indicate success: 200 OK is the most common, and 201 Created is returned when a new resource has been created. Codes in the 4xx range indicate a client error. A server returns 400 Bad Request when the request is malformed, and 401 Unauthorized when the request lacks valid authentication credentials; in that case the response should include a WWW-Authenticate header describing how to authenticate. 403 Forbidden means that the server understood who the client is but refuses to authorize the action. 422 Unprocessable Content is used when the syntax of the request is correct but its content fails validation. Codes in the 5xx range indicate a server error: 500 Internal Server Error is a generic failure, and 503 Service Unavailable means that the server is temporarily unable to handle the request, for example while it is starting up or overloaded.
items.question: Which status code is returned when a new resource has been created?

items.context: Adam is an algorithm for first-order gradient-based optimization of stochastic objective functions, introduced by Diederik Kingma and Jimmy Ba in 2014. The name is derived from adaptive moment estimation. Adam keeps an exponential moving average of the gradient, called the first moment, and of the squared gradient, called the second moment. Because both averages are initialized at zero, they are biased towards zero during the first steps, so the algorithm applies a bias correction. The paper recommends a learning rate of 0.001, decay rates of 0.9 for the first moment and 0.999 for the second moment, and an epsilon of 10^-8. A popular variant, AdamW, decouples weight decay from the gradient update and is the default optimizer for fine-tuning Transformer models.
items.question: Who introduced Adam?

items.context: Docker is a platform for packaging applications into containers. It was released as open-source software in 2013 by the company dotCloud, which later renamed itself Docker, Inc. A container bundles an application with its libraries and configuration, but unlike a virtual machine it does not include a full guest operating system: all containers on a host share the host's kernel. This makes containers lighter and faster to start than virtual machines. Images are built from a text file called a Dockerfile, in which each instruction creates a new read-only layer. Layers are cached, so rebuilding an image after a small change only rebuilds the layers that follow the change. A running instance of an image is called a container.
items.question: In what year was Docker released as open-source software?

items.context: Dropout is a regularization technique for neural networks proposed by Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton and colleagues, and published in the Journal of Machine Learning Research in 2014. During training, each unit is temporarily removed from the network with a fixed probability, together with its incoming and outgoing connections. This prevents units from co-adapting too much and forces the network to learn more robust features. The authors found that retaining hidden units with a probability of 0.5 works well for a wide range of networks, while input units should be retained with a probability closer to 1. At test time no units are dropped; instead, the outgoing weights of each unit are multiplied by the probability with which it was retained during training.
items.question: In which journal was dropout published?

answers.text: the Journal of Machine Learning Research

items.context:
For most of the 2000s, computer vision relied on hand-designed features such as SIFT and HOG, which were extracted from images and passed to a separate classifier. Progress was measured on benchmarks that were small by modern standards, and improvements from one year to the next were often only a few percentage points.

This changed with ImageNet, a dataset of more than 14 million labeled images created by a project led by Fei-Fei Li. Its yearly competition, the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC), used a subset of about 1.2 million training images in 1,000 categories. In 2012, a convolutional neural network called AlexNet, developed by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, won the challenge with a top-5 error of 15.3%, compared with 26.2% for the second-best entry. AlexNet was trained on two GPUs and used ReLU activations and dropout, ideas that quickly became standard.

In the following years, networks became deeper. VGG, from the Visual Geometry Group at the University of Oxford, showed in 2014 that stacking many small 3x3 convolutions in networks of 16 or 19 layers improved accuracy. However, simply adding layers eventually made results worse: very deep plain networks were harder to optimize, and their training error went up instead of down.

Also in 2014, GoogLeNet, from Google, won the classification task with its Inception modules, which apply convolutions of several sizes in parallel and concatenate the results. Despite being deeper than AlexNet, it used about 12 times fewer parameters.

Residual networks, or ResNets, solved this degradation problem. Proposed in 2015 by Kaiming He and colleagues at Microsoft Research, they add shortcut connections that skip one or more layers, so that each block only has to learn a residual function with respect to its input. With these connections, the authors trained networks with 152 layers, and an ensemble of ResNets won ILSVRC 2015 with a top-5 error of 3.57%. Batch normalization, introduced the same year by Sergey Ioffe and Christian Szegedy, normalizes the activations of each layer over a mini-batch and was used throughout these networks to stabilize training.

Networks pre-trained on ImageNet also became the standard starting point for other tasks. Instead of training from scratch, practitioners take a network trained on ImageNet, replace its final classification layer, and fine-tune it on a smaller dataset, a practice known as transfer learning.

The next shift came from natural language processing. In 2020, the Vision Transformer (ViT) applied a standard Transformer encoder directly to images. It splits an image into patches of 16x16 pixels, flattens each patch into a vector, adds a position embedding, and processes the resulting sequence exactly like a sequence of word tokens. When pre-trained on very large datasets, ViT matched or exceeded the best convolutional networks, although with less data it tended to perform worse, because it lacks the built-in assumptions about locality that convolutions provide.
items.question: Who led the project that created ImageNet?

It splits an image into patches of 16x16 pixels, flattens each patch into a vector, adds a position embedding, and processes the resulting sequence exactly like a sequence of word tokens. When pre-trained on very large datasets, ViT matched or exceeded the best convolutional networks, although with less data it tended to perform worse, because it lacks the built-in assumptions about locality that convolutions provide.

items.context:
For most of the 2000s, computer vision relied on hand-designed features such as SIFT and HOG, which were extracted from images and passed to a separate classifier. Progress was measured on benchmarks that were small by modern standards, and improvements from one year to the next were often only a few percentage points.

This changed with ImageNet, a dataset of more than 14 million labeled images created by a project led by Fei-Fei Li. Its yearly competition, the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC), used a subset of about 1.2 million training images in 1,000 categories. In 2012, a convolutional neural network called AlexNet, developed by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, won the challenge with a top-5 error of 15.3%, compared with 26.2% for the second-best entry. AlexNet was trained on two GPUs and used ReLU activations and dropout, ideas that quickly became standard.

In the following years, networks became deeper. VGG, from the Visual Geometry Group at the University of Oxford, showed in 2014 that stacking many small 3x3 convolutions in networks of 16 or 19 layers improved accuracy. However, simply adding layers eventually made results worse: very deep plain networks were harder to optimize, and their training error went up instead of down.

Also in 2014, GoogLeNet, from Google, won the classification task with its Inception modules, which apply convolutions of several sizes in parallel and concatenate the results. Despite being deeper than AlexNet, it used about 12 times fewer parameters.

Residual networks, or ResNets, solved this degradation problem. Proposed in 2015 by Kaiming He and colleagues at Microsoft Research, they add shortcut connections that skip one or more layers, so that each block only has to learn a residual function with respect to its input. With these connections, the authors trained networks with 152 layers, and an ensemble of ResNets won ILSVRC 2015 with a top-5 error of 3.57%. Batch normalization, introduced the same year by Sergey Ioffe and Christian Szegedy, normalizes the activations of each layer over a mini-batch and was used throughout these networks to stabilize training.

Networks pre-trained on ImageNet also became the standard starting point for other tasks. Instead of training from scratch, practitioners take a network trained on ImageNet, replace its final classification layer, and fine-tune it on a smaller dataset, a practice known as transfer learning.

The next shift came from natural language processing. In 2020, the Vision Transformer (ViT) applied a standard Transformer encoder directly to images. It splits an image into patches of 16x16 pixels, flattens each patch into a vector, adds a position embedding, and processes the resulting sequence exactly like a sequence of word tokens. When pre-trained on very large datasets, ViT matched or exceeded the best convolutional networks, although with less data it tended to perform worse, because it lacks the built-in assumptions about locality that convolutions provide.
